title: Cut: reconstitution and handoffs, with a ledger held by construction
situation: 0074 had the capability perform every transition, but leaned on agents calling verbs. The harness already reports agent lifecycle events (a subagent dispatched, started, finished, its result returned), and git offers natural boundaries (a commit, a merge) where a hook can check and record. The work package log is untracked and shared by every worktree of a host, so parallel cuts in separate worktrees read one another's state. The architect has also recorded acceptances and decisions about a cut on dev while that cut's work sat unmerged in its worktree, so the journal claimed what dev did not hold.
decision: One cut. (1) A computed overview of each context, read first at every reconstitution. (2) The workflow ships as its self-explaining capabilities. (3) The ledger of cuts and work packages is held by construction. The cratylus extension appends a work package's lifecycle from the harness's own agent lifecycle events: dispatched when its builder is dispatched, returned when the builder returns, approved when its assayers' verdicts return. A commit hook refuses a commit whose structured message does not name its cut and work package, records the commit in the ledger, and refuses one whose changes or claimed state disagree with the state the ledger computes at that moment. Each event carries a transition id, so a repeat is refused; events are entries of their own, created exclusively and versioned with the branch they belong to. (4) Every ledger, the concept journal's included, is read and appended in the worktree the agent works in, so it sees its own branch's state; a cut's entries, acceptances and decisions about it included, are made on the cut's branch and land with its merge. (5) Typed handoffs, with example 19 first. (6) The architect as principal (0070). (7) Every agent's default tools (0068).
consequences: Next in 0072's order. From now on the architect records a cut's acceptance on that cut's branch, before it is merged.
